verdict.summary:
# FMCSA Short-Haul (RODS) Exception — 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)

## 1. Answer

| Ask | Threshold | Unit | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Radius within which the driver must operate, measured from the normal work reporting location | **150** | air miles (regulation's own equivalent: 172.6 statute miles) | 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i) |
| 2. Consecutive hours within which the driver must return and be released from work | **14** | consecutive hours | 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii) |

Both values are current law as of the eCFR fetch. A driver meeting all of §395.1(e)(1) is exempt from the record-of-duty-status requirement (§395.8) and the supporting-documents requirement (§395.11).

## 2. Governing text (verbatim)

> **(e) Short-haul operations —**
> **(1) 150 air-mile radius driver.** A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
> (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
> (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
> (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
> (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
> (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) the time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) the total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) the time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) the total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with §395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.

Corroboration — FMCSA, *Summary of Hours of Service Regulations* (last updated 2022-03-28): "A driver is exempt from the requirements of §395.8 and §395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours. Drivers using the short-haul exception in §395.1(e)(1) must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours, and stay within a 150 air-mile radius of the work reporting location."

## 3. How each threshold is measured

### 3.1 The radius (150 air miles)

- **Origin point.** The "normal work reporting location." Part 395 does not separately define the term; the regulation supplies its own gloss at §395.1(e)(2)(ii): "the location where the driver reports to and is released from work, i.e., the normal work reporting location." It is a fixed, designated location (terminal, yard, drop lot), not the driver's residence and not wherever the driver happens to be dispatched from on a given day.
- **Metric.** Air miles = straight-line (great-circle) distance, **not** road miles and not route distance. The regulation itself parenthesizes the conversion: 150 air miles = **172.6 statute miles**. (150 × 1.15078 = 172.617; the same 1.15078 factor converts the predecessor provision's "100 air-mile radius (115 statute miles)." In this provision an "air mile" is being converted as a nautical mile.)
- **Which number to compare against.** Two equivalent formulations, and the carrier must not mix them:
  - Working in air miles (nautical, R = 3440.065 nmi): require d ≤ **150**.
  - Working in statute miles (mean Earth radius R = 3958.761 mi): require d ≤ **172.6**.
- **Conservative fallback.** Many carriers apply a flat 150 *statute*-mile great-circle test. That is stricter than the rule and therefore never non-compliant; it is a safe default where the carrier does not want to defend the 172.6 figure. State which convention the carrier uses in its policy so auditors see a consistent test.
- **Haversine, the standard computation:**

  ```
  phi1, lam1 = radians(lat_base), radians(lon_base)
  phi2, lam2 = radians(lat_point), radians(lon_point)
  dphi = phi2 - phi1
  dlam = lam2 - lam1
  a = sin(dphi/2)^2 + cos(phi1)*cos(phi2)*sin(dlam/2)^2
  c = 2*asin(min(1, sqrt(a)))
  d_nm    = 3440.065 * c        # compare to 150
  d_stat  = 3958.761 * c        # compare to 172.6
  ```

- **Worked checks** (base = Chicago, 41.8781 N, −87.6298 W):

  | Point | d (statute mi) | d (air miles) | Verdict vs 150 air miles |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Grand Rapids, MI (42.9634, −85.6681) | 125.0 | 108.6 | PASS |
  | Due north, 44.30 N, same longitude | 167.3 | 145.4 | PASS (would fail a naive 150-statute-mile test — this is the case that shows why the unit matters) |
  | Due north, 44.60 N, same longitude | 187.9 | 163.3 | FAIL |

  Rule of thumb for sanity-checking: 1° of latitude ≈ 69.05 statute miles ≈ 60 air miles, so the 150-air-mile circle is ≈ 2.5° of latitude in radius.
- **Operational test.** The radius is not a check on the destination alone. Every point the vehicle reaches during the duty tour must lie inside the circle; a single out-of-radius stop defeats the exception for that day.

### 3.2 The 14 consecutive hours

- **Clock start.** The moment the driver comes on duty (reports for duty) at the normal work reporting location.
- **Clock end.** The moment the carrier releases the driver from duty, **at the normal work reporting location**. Both conditions in §395.1(e)(1)(ii) must be satisfied — return *and* release — so a driver who is back at the terminal at hour 13 but still on duty until hour 15 has failed the test.
- **Elapsed time, not accumulated duty time.** The 14 hours run continuously. Off-duty time taken mid-tour does not pause or extend the clock — same structure as the §395.3(a)(2) 14-hour window. A driver on duty 05:30 must be back and released no later than 19:30.
- **"Released from work" means released from duty entirely** — not merely off duty for a break within a shift. The driver's duty tour is over and the driver is at the normal work reporting location.
- **Driver-salesperson carve-out.** §395.1(e)(1)(ii) begins "except a driver-salesperson." For a driver who qualifies as a driver-salesperson, the return-and-release-within-14-hours condition does not apply; the radius and the off-duty conditions still do, and §395.3 still applies in full. If the driver is not a driver-salesperson, 14 hours governs without exception.

## 4. Day-level compliance procedure

Run this for each duty tour. The exception is all-or-nothing: "If even one of the qualifications is not met, then all of the standard hours of service rules apply" (FMCSA CSA Safety Planner, §6.4.4).

1. **Designate the normal work reporting location** in writing before the tour (address + lat/lon), and record it in the driver's file.
2. **Capture t0** — time the driver reports for duty at that location.
3. **Capture every stop/waypoint** with coordinates (ELD or GPS breadcrumb, or dispatch itinerary).
4. **Test A — radius.** For each waypoint compute d to the base per §3.1. If any d > 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles), the tour fails the exception.
5. **Test B — release.** Confirm the driver is physically at the base and released from duty at t ≤ t0 + 14 h. If not, the tour fails the exception.
6. **Test C — rest.** Confirm ≥10 consecutive hours off duty (property-carrying) or ≥8 (passenger-carrying) separating this tour from the prior one.
7. **Test D — records.** Confirm the carrier captured and will retain for 6 months: report-for-duty time, total hours on duty, release-from-duty time, and (for first-time/intermittent drivers) the preceding-7-days total under §395.8(j)(2).
8. **Test E — underlying HOS.** Independently confirm §395.3 compliance: 11-hour driving limit, 14-hour window, 30-minute break after 8 cumulative driving hours, 60/70-hour limit. The exception waives none of these.
9. **Record the outcome** (pass/fail + the computed d and the release timestamp) so the determination is auditable.

**No consecutive-day cap.** §395.1(e)(1) contains no limit on how many consecutive days a driver may use the exception. A driver may use it every duty tour provided steps 1–9 pass each time. The 60/70-hour limit in §395.3(b) still constrains total weekly duty.

## 5. What the exception does and does not waive

| Waived | Not waived |
|---|---|
| §395.8 — record of duty status | §395.3 — 11-hour driving, 14-hour window, 30-minute break, 60/70-hour |
| §395.11 — supporting documents | §395.1(e)(1)(i)–(iv) — the exception's own conditions |
| ELD use (the ELD mandate attaches to drivers required to keep RODS; short-haul drivers under (e)(1) are not, per ELD FAQ17: "Drivers who use the short-haul, timecard exceptions are not required to keep records of duty status (RODS) or use ELDs") | Carrier time-record duty — 6 months, four data elements |

## 6. Consequences of a failed day

- The standard HOS rules apply in full for that tour, and a **RODS must be prepared for that day** under §395.8.
- The driver may still be outside the ELD mandate if the driver is required to keep RODS **not more than 8 days within any 30-day period** (ELD FAQ17); such a driver must still prepare RODS by paper log, AOBRD, or logging software. Exceed 8 RODS days in 30 and an ELD is required.
- The carrier's time records must still exist for the day (they are what proves the exception was or was not used), retained 6 months.

## 7. Version control and common conflations (why 150/14 and not 100/12)

- **100 air miles / 12 hours is the pre-2020 text of §395.1(e)(1).** The short-haul exception was raised to 150 air miles / 14 hours by the hours-of-service final rule published June 2020 (85 FR 33396), effective September 29, 2020. Any page still showing 100/12 for the RODS short-haul exception is stale. One source surfaced during this research (the New Entrant page at `ai.fmcsa.dot.gov/test/...`) does still show "100 air-mile radius drivers ... released from work within 12 consecutive hours" — it sits under a `/test/` path (a staging environment) and is superseded by the eCFR text and by FMCSA's own Summary of Hours of Service Regulations page (updated 2022-03-28), both of which state 150/14. Do not use 100/12.
- **§395.1(e)(2) — non-CDL property-carrying short haul.** Also a 150 air-mile radius and also a RODS exemption, but a *distinct* provision with a different driving structure: no driving after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days and after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7. If the driver does not require a CDL, evaluate (e)(2) as well; it does not change the radius answer (still 150 air miles) but it changes the hours answer.
- **§395.1(p) — motion picture production.** 100 air-mile radius, but it exempts from §395.3(a) only, not from RODS. A 100-air-mile figure appearing in Part 395 today belongs to this provision or to a superseded version of (e)(1).
- **150 air-mile provisions that are not RODS exemptions.** The radius figure also appears in hours exemptions (e.g., the agricultural-commodity provisions). Those relieve HOS limits, not the RODS requirement; the driver still logs. Radius alone never establishes the RODS exception.

## 8. One-line answer for the record

Under 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), a driver is relieved of the RODS requirement only if the driver operates **within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location** and **returns to that location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours** of coming on duty.

quotes.whole:
Friday, November 15, 2024
WASHINGTON – The Federal Aviation Administration updated its BasicMed regulations to allow pilots to operate larger aircraft and carry more passengers.
BasicMed, which took effect in 2017, allows pilots to fly without holding an FAA medical certificate provided they meet certain conditions.
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required the FAA to expand BasicMed to:
Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six.
Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.
Allow pilot examiners to conduct flight checks using BasicMed in aircraft that are covered by the BasicMed rule. Information for examiners is available here.
Pilots must meet specific conditions to operate under BasicMed. Among other things, they must have held a valid medical certificate at some point after July 14, 2006; the most recent medical certificate cannot have been denied, revoked, or suspended; they must complete a medical exam by a state-licensed physician; they must complete an online medical education course; and they must hold a valid U.S. driver’s license.

quotes.whole:
3.1 What Do I Need to Fly Under BasicMed?
1. Hold a current and valid U.S. driver’s license.
2. Hold or have held a medical certificate issued by the FAA at any point after
July 14, 2006.
3. Answer the health questions on the Comprehensive Medical Examination
Checklist (CMEC).
4. Get your physical examination by any State-licensed physician, and have that
physician complete the CMEC (be sure to keep the CMEC).
5. Take the BasicMed online medical education course. Keep the course
completion document issued to you by the course provider.
3.2 What Are My BasicMed Privileges? You can conduct any operation that you would
otherwise be able to conduct using your pilot certificate and a third-class medical
certificate, except you are limited to:
1. Fly with no more than five passengers.
2. Fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than
6,000 lbs.
3. Fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants.
4. Flights within the United States, at an indicated airspeed of 250 knots or less,
and at an altitude at or below 18,000 feet mean sea level (MSL).
5. You may not fly for compensation or hire.
3.3 What Do I Need to Maintain My BasicMed Privileges?

verdict.summary:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — CURRENT RULE (US, 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) as expanded by the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Pub. L. 118-63 § 828)

ANSWERS
1. Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 lb — maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW). Exception: transport category helicopters remain at 6,000 lb.
2. Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7 (including the pilot and any required flightcrew).
3. Passengers on board: 6.

All three limits apply simultaneously to the same flight; an aircraft and operation must satisfy every one of them, not the most permissive.

EFFECTIVE DATE / VERSION — WHY THESE NUMBERS AND NOT THE OLD ONES
The expanded limits apply to operations on or after November 12, 2024. Before that date the limits were 6,000 lb MTOW, 6 occupants authorized, and 5 passengers on board. Those older figures are still widely reproduced (FAA AC 68-1A dated 5/3/17; FAA Safety Briefing, July/August 2017) and are superseded. FAA Notice N 8000.386 states both sets side by side and dates the change:
  • "The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than six occupants, the aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of no more than 6,000 pounds, and the aircraft is operated with no more than five passengers on board."
  • "Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024: the aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, the aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and the aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board."
The FAA BasicMed page as currently published states the same: "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants / Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds / Carries not more than six passengers." The FAA newsroom release of November 15, 2024 confirms the rulemaking and adds the helicopter carve-out: "Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six. Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters."

DEFINITIONS THAT DECIDE COMPLIANCE
• "Maximum takeoff weight" = maximum certificated takeoff weight, a design-approval value found in the Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS), the AFM/POH limitations section, or the applicable STC — not a weight-and-balance computation for a particular flight. An aircraft certificated at 12,500 lb or less qualifies even if it is normally operated well below that; an aircraft certificated above 12,500 lb does not qualify even if it is light that day.
• "Authorized to carry" = the number of occupants the aircraft's design approval permits, i.e. type certificate, amended TC, or STC — not the number of seats currently installed and not the number of people actually on board. FAA AC 68-1A § 5.1.1–5.1.2: "The aircraft must be authorized by the FAA to carry not more than six occupants... For type certificated aircraft, the aircraft's design approval would authorize the number of occupants the aircraft may carry and would contain the maximum certificated takeoff weight." The BasicMed FAQ makes the same point with the Piper PA-32 family: a PA-32-260/300 with six seats and no seven-seat kit qualifies; the same airframe converted with Piper Kit 69072-3 to seven seats also now qualifies under the seven-occupant limit, but a model whose type certificate authorizes more than the limit does not qualify merely because seats were removed — it requires an STC restricting the type design.
• "Passengers on board" = persons actually carried other than the pilot and any required flightcrew, counted at departure. Occupants (limit 7) and passengers (limit 6) are separate tests.

OPERATING LIMITS THAT TRAVEL WITH THESE AIRCRAFT LIMITS (unchanged)
Flights must remain within the United States (plus jurisdictions where BasicMed is recognized), at or below 18,000 ft MSL, at an indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots, and not for compensation or hire. The limitations apply to the entire flight: a pilot exercising BasicMed privileges may not act as PIC for any portion of a flight that exceeds them, even if another pilot on board holds a medical certificate.

HOW TO VERIFY A SPECIFIC AIRCRAFT
1. Pull the TCDS (or STC/ATC) and read the maximum certificated takeoff weight and the approved occupant/seating configuration. 2. Compare MTOW to 12,500 lb (6,000 lb if the aircraft is a transport category helicopter). 3. Compare the type-certificated occupant count to 7 — do not count installed seats. 4. Plan the load so that no more than 6 passengers are aboard. 5. Confirm the other operating limits (airspace, altitude, speed, compensation) for the whole flight.

WORKED EXAMPLES (each satisfies or fails on the stated test)
• Cessna 172S — MTOW 2,550 lb; certificated for 4 occupants. Compliant.
• Piper PA-32-300 Cherokee Six — MTOW 3,400 lb; TCDS A3SO authorizes 6 seats, or 7 with Piper Kit 69072-3. Compliant either way under the current rule; carry no more than 6 passengers.
• Socata TBM 700 — MTOW 6,579 lb; 6 occupants. Compliant now; not compliant before November 12, 2024 (weight).
• Cessna 208 Caravan — MTOW 8,000 lb (weight passes) but certificated to carry more than 7 occupants in passenger configurations (occupant test fails). Not compliant unless the specific aircraft's design approval restricts it to 7 or fewer occupants. This illustrates that passing the weight test alone is not enough.
• Pilatus PC-12/47 — MTOW 9,920 lb (weight passes); up to 9 passengers (occupant and passenger tests fail). Not compliant.
• Transport category helicopter (e.g., Sikorsky S-76) — MTOW above 6,000 lb. Not compliant: the weight increase to 12,500 lb expressly excludes transport category helicopters, so the 6,000 lb ceiling still governs them.

VERIFICATION ITEM (flagged, not asserted)
For experimental airworthiness certificates, AC 68-1A cites 14 CFR 91.319(j) as capping BasicMed operations at six occupants. That text predates the 2024 expansion and I have no fetched passage showing a conforming amendment. Before operating an experimental aircraft under BasicMed with seven occupants, confirm the current text of § 91.319(j); the three answers above are stated for the general rule in § 61.113(i)(1) and are unaffected by this open item.

Editorial Note on Part 395




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.


Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:




(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:




(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or






(2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.








(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or





(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.

verdict.summary:
**Federal hours-of-service limits for a passenger-carrying CMV driver (49 CFR 395.5)**

**Scope and assumptions**
- The driver operates a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle in interstate commerce — the motorcoach case in the request.
- The governing rule is the federal FMCSA passenger-carrying HOS rule, 49 CFR 395.5. The property-carrying rule in 49 CFR 395.3 does **not** apply to this vehicle class.
- The standard limits are stated; the exceptions and exemptions in 49 CFR 395.1 can alter application in specific circumstances (e.g., adverse driving conditions, sleeper-berth split), but they do not change the baseline answers below.
- State intrastate passenger-carrier rules may be stricter; the federal rule is the baseline for interstate operation.

**Direct answers**

| Ask | Answer | Regulatory basis | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|---|
| 1. How many hours may they drive? | **10 hours** | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) | A driver may not drive more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty. The 10 hours is cumulative driving time in the duty period; it need not be consecutive. Once 10 hours of driving is reached, no further driving until another 8 consecutive hours off duty. |
| 2. After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8 hours** | 49 CFR 395.5(a) | Before driving, the driver must have at least 8 consecutive hours off duty. The 8 hours must be consecutive and must contain no on-duty or driving time. It may consist of off-duty time, sleeper-berth time, or a combination, subject to the sleeper-berth provision in 49 CFR 395.1(g)(3). |
| 3. After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | **15 hours** | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(2) | A driver may not drive for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty. After 15 on-duty hours, the driver may perform non-driving work but may not drive again until another 8 consecutive hours off duty. |

**How the three limits interact**
- They are independent limits; the driver must satisfy all three. The 10-hour driving limit is the driving-time cap. The 15-hour limit is the total on-duty cap. The 8-hour off-duty period is the reset that starts a new driving/duty period.
- The 15-hour limit is measured in **on-duty hours**, not simply elapsed clock hours. FMCSA's passenger-carrier guidance explains that off-duty time taken during the day, such as a lunch break, does not count toward the 15-hour on-duty limit. Thus a duty period can span more than 15 clock hours if non-duty breaks are taken, but the driver still cannot drive after accumulating 15 on-duty hours.
- The 10-hour driving limit is not reset by a mid-day off-duty break. Only 8 consecutive hours off duty (or the regulatory sleeper-berth equivalent) resets the 10-hour driving allowance.
- The 8 consecutive hours must be free of on-duty and driving time. A shorter break, or a break interrupted by duty, does not satisfy the reset.

**Weekly limits (context, not part of the three asks)**
49 CFR 395.5(b) separately prohibits driving after:
- **60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days**, if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- **70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days**, if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.
These weekly caps are additional to the 10-hour and 15-hour limits and are not answers to asks 1–3.

**Common errors to avoid**
- Do not use the property-carrying figures (11-hour driving, 14-hour on-duty window, 10 consecutive hours off duty). Those are in 49 CFR 395.3 and apply to property-carrying CMVs, not passenger-carrying CMVs.
- Do not describe the passenger-carrier 15-hour limit as a 15-hour elapsed window. It is 15 hours **on duty** following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
- Do not treat a mid-day break as satisfying the 8-consecutive-hour off-duty requirement. The 8 hours must be consecutive and free of duty.
- Do not assume the federal rule is the only rule. A state may impose stricter intrastate passenger-carrier limits.

**Source text (49 CFR 395.5(a), current eCFR text)**
> No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle: (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.

**Bottom line**
For a passenger-carrying CMV driver such as a motorcoach driver under the federal interstate rule: **10 hours of driving**, after **8 consecutive hours off duty**, and **no driving after 15 hours on duty** following that 8-hour off-duty period.

Off-Duty Time
“Off-duty time” is not speciﬁcally deﬁned in the regulations. In effect, it is any time that is not “driving time,” “on-duty time,” or “sleeper berth” as deﬁned in § 395.2.
The following guidelines must be met before a driver is considered off duty for meal and other routine stops made during a work shift:
The driver must be relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the bus or passenger-carrying CMV, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage and freight that it may be transporting.
During the stop, and for the duration of the stop, the driver must be

considered off duty for the entire period.
Relief Drivers
On long-distance trips requiring straight-through driving, motorcoach companies may send a relief driver ahead.
In cases when the driver is driven or uses public transportation to get to a layover location, and the driver has 8 consecutive hours off duty after arriving, travel time may be recorded as off duty.
If the CMV driver drives him/herself in a non-CMV, time spent driving the non-CMV to a layover location must be recorded as on duty, not driving.

Calendar day   means the period of elapsed time, using Coordinated Universal Time or local time, that begins at midnight and ends 24 hours later at the next midnight.
Duty period   means the period of elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder. The time is calculated using either Coordinated Universal Time or local time to reflect the total elapsed time.
Flight attendant   means an individual, other than a flight crewmember, who is assigned by the certificate holder, in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the certificate holder's operations specifications or in addition to that minimum complement, to duty in an aircraft during flight time and whose duties include but are not necessarily limited to cabin-safety-related responsibilities.
Rest period   means the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise.

Prepared by: Alex Zektser, Attorney, for AGC-220 
Subject: Applicability of part 13 5 flight, duty, and rest rules to flight attendants 
assigned in addition to the minimally-required crew complement 
This is in response to your July 6, 2011 memorandum requesting an interpretation as to 
the applicability of the flight, duty, and rest regulations of 14 C.F.R. § 135.273. In your 
memorandum, you state that some carriers operating under part 135 voluntarily add ilight 
attendant personnel to flights in aircraft with 19 seats or less by assigning cabin safety 
procedures and responsibilities to those personnel. 1 You ask whether these voluntarily­
added flight attendants are subject to the flight, duty, and rest regulations of§ 135.273. 
Subsection 135.273(a) contains a set of definitions that are used throughout§ 135.273. 
This subsection defines a "flight attendant" as either: 
(1) "an individual other than a flight crewmember, who is assigned by the certificate 
holder, in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the 
certificate holder's operations specifications;" or 
(2) an individual who is assigned to duty on an aircraft during flight time in addition 
to the minimum crew complement and "whose duties include but are not 
necessarily limited to cabin-safety-related responsibilities." 
Thus , under the regulatory excerpt in number (2) above, an individual is a flight attendant 
if they are assigned to a flight and are assigned cabin-safety related responsibilities 
during flight time. For purposes of this provision, it is irrelevant that the individual is not 
required to be assigned to that flight, as this portion of the "flight attendant" definition 
encompasses individuals who are assigned to the flight in addition to the minimally-
1 
Flight attendants are not required for part 135 operations unless the aircraft has a passenger seating 
configuration of more than 19 people. See 14 C.F.R. § 135.107. However, this does not preclude an 
operator from voluntarily assigning flight attendants to a flight. 
1 
required crew. Thus, if an operator voluntarily assigns individuals to a crew on a part 
135 operation and assigns cabin-safety-related responsibilities to those individuals during 
flight time, then those individuals are "flight attendants" for purposes of§ 135.273. 
Subsections 135.273(b) and (c) specify a set of flight, duty and rest rules that are 
applicable to flight attendants. These subsections do not distinguish between different 
types of flight attendants. Consequently, any individual on a part 135 operation who fits 
the flight-attendant definition of§ 135.273(a) is subject to the flight, duty, and rest rules 
of§ 135.273. This means that flight attendants who are assigned to a flight in addition to 
the minimum crew complement are subject to the flight, duty, and rest rules of 
§ 135.273. 2 
2 
In a previous interpretation, the FAA also stated that flight attendants voluntarily added to a part 135 
flight by an operator are subject to the flight attendant training and testing requirements of part 135. See 
Letter to Kevin F. Schehr from Rebecca MacPherson, Assistant Chief Counsel for Regulations (Sep. 22, 
2008).

verdict.summary:
ANSWER
1) After a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, a Part 135 certificate holder must give the flight attendant a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. 14 C.F.R. § 135.273(b)(2).
2) That rest may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours only if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours, scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and occurring between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period. § 135.273(b)(3).

REGULATORY BASIS AND APPLICABILITY
- Section 135.273 applies to flight attendants in all operations conducted under Part 135. Section 135.263(e). It therefore applies to an on-demand charter operator; the non-scheduled flightcrew rules in §§ 135.267 and 135.269 do not displace § 135.273 for a flight attendant.
- A 'flight attendant' is an individual, other than a flightcrewmember, assigned by the certificate holder under the required minimum crew complement in the operations specifications or in addition to that complement, to duty in an aircraft during flight time, whose duties include cabin-safety-related responsibilities. § 135.273(a). The FAA legal interpretation dated June 10, 2014 (AGC-220) confirms that voluntarily added flight attendants with cabin-safety duties are covered even in aircraft with 19 or fewer seats.
- 'Rest period' means the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise. § 135.273(a).
- No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant a duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by § 135.273, and no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to any duty during a required rest period. § 135.273(b)(10)-(11).

OPERATIVE REGULATORY TEXT
§ 135.273(b)(2): 'Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'
§ 135.273(b)(3): 'The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'

ANALYSIS AND COMPLIANCE STEPS
- Baseline: schedule at least 9 consecutive hours of rest, positioned between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the next duty period.
- Reduced rest: schedule or reduce to 8 consecutive hours only if the operator also provides a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours. That subsequent rest must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. If any condition is not met, the 9-hour rest is required.
- The 8-hour figure is a floor. Section 135.273(b)(3) does not permit reduction below 8 consecutive hours.
- Do not use the 10-hour provision in § 135.273(b)(8) for this question. Section 135.273(b)(8) permits a rest to be scheduled or reduced to 10 consecutive hours with a subsequent 14-hour rest, but it applies to the rest required under § 135.273(b)(7), not to the rest required after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less. The 14-hour/24-hour duty restriction in § 135.273(b)(9) is likewise tied to a § 135.273(b)(8) 10-hour reduction, not to the § 135.273(b)(3) 8-hour reduction.
- If actual duty exceeds 14 hours, re-evaluate under § 135.273(b)(4)-(8); the answer above is for a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less.
- If the operator has an approved election under § 135.273(c) to apply flightcrewmember duty and rest rules to flight attendants, the result may differ. That election requires written procedures approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the operations specifications. Absent such an election, the 9-hour/8-hour rule above applies.
- If the individual is serving as a flightcrewmember rather than a flight attendant, § 135.267 (for on-demand operations) or other flightcrew rules apply, not this flight-attendant answer.

TIMING EXAMPLE
If the reduced 8-hour rest begins at 22:00, the subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours must begin no later than 22:00 the following day, which is 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period, and must be positioned as required between the duty periods. If no reduction is used, the default is at least 9 consecutive hours free of all responsibility for work or duty.

BOTTOM LINE
Baseline: 9 consecutive hours. Permitted reduction: 8 consecutive hours, but only with the required subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours and the 24-hour timing condition in § 135.273(b)(3).

2.1.  Document Organization
The HTTP/2 specification is split into four parts:
o  Starting HTTP/2 (Section 3) covers how an HTTP/2 connection is
initiated.
o  The frame (Section 4) and stream (Section 5) layers describe the
way HTTP/2 frames are structured and formed into multiplexed
streams.
o  Frame (Section 6) and error (Section 7) definitions include
details of the frame and error types used in HTTP/2.
o  HTTP mappings (Section 8) and additional requirements (Section 9)
describe how HTTP semantics are expressed using frames and
streams.
While some of the frame and stream layer concepts are isolated from
HTTP, this specification does not define a completely generic frame
layer.  The frame and stream layers are tailored to the needs of the
HTTP protocol and server push.

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",
"SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this

quotes.whole:
Appendix B. Changes from RFC 7540
This revision includes the following substantive changes:
Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes.
The priority scheme defined in RFC 7540 is deprecated. Definitions for the format of the PRIORITY frame and the priority fields in the HEADERS frame have been retained, plus the rules governing when PRIORITY frames can be sent and received, but the semantics of these fields are only described in RFC 7540. The priority signaling scheme from RFC 7540 was not successful. Using the simpler signaling in [HTTP-PRIORITY] is recommended.
The HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism is deprecated and no longer specified in this document. It was never widely deployed, with plaintext HTTP/2 users choosing to use the prior-knowledge implementation instead.
Validation for field names and values has been narrowed. The validation that is mandatory for intermediaries is precisely defined, and error reporting for requests has been amended to encourage sending 400-series status codes.
The ranges of codepoints for settings and frame types that were reserved for Experimental Use are now available for general use.

# HTTP/2: current specification and what it obsoletes

## Answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113** |
| RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113 | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** |

## 1. Current specification — RFC 9113

- **Number:** RFC 9113
- **Title:** HTTP/2
- **Authors/Editors:** M. Thomson, Ed. (Mozilla); C. Benfield, Ed. (Apple Inc.)
- **Publication date:** June 2022
- **Stream / category:** IETF, Standards Track (Proposed Standard)
- **ISSN:** 2070-1721
- **Canonical citation:** M. Thomson, Ed. and C. Benfield, Ed., "HTTP/2", RFC 9113, DOI 10.17487/RFC9113, June 2022, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113>.

The document's own header block reads, verbatim:

```
Stream:   Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)
RFC:      9113
Obsoletes: 7540, 8740
Category:  Standards Track
Published: June 2022
ISSN:      2070-1721
```

and its abstract states: "This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2). ... This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

## 2. RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113

Exactly two, as listed in RFC 9113's `Obsoletes:` header and repeated in its abstract:

| Obsoleted RFC | Title | Original status | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RFC 7540** | Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2) | Proposed Standard, May 2015 (Belshe, Peon, Thomson, Eds.) | The original HTTP/2 specification. Its errata page now carries "⚠ This RFC has been obsoleted! Obsoleted by: RFC9113; Updated by: RFC8740". |
| **RFC 8740** | Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2 | Proposed Standard, February 2020 (D. Benjamin) | It had *updated* RFC 7540 (forbidding TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication); RFC 9113 folded that requirement in and obsoletes RFC 8740 as a separate document. RFC 9113 Appendix B: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes." |

Corroboration from independent directions (all three agree):
- RFC Editor info page for RFC 9113 — `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`.
- RFC Editor HTTP/2 subject page — RFC 7540 marked "Obsoleted by RFC 9113"; RFC 8740 marked "Obsoleted by RFC 9113".
- RFC 7540 errata search page — "Obsoleted by: RFC9113 / Updated by: RFC8740".

## 3. Scope boundaries (what is *not* obsoleted)

Stated explicitly so the answer is not over-read:

- **RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2)** is **not** obsoleted by RFC 9113; it remains the compression specification referenced by HTTP/2.
- **HTTP/2 extension documents are not obsoleted:** RFC 8441 (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2), RFC 8336 (The ORIGIN HTTP/2 Frame), RFC 8164 (Opportunistic Security for HTTP/2, Historic) all remain as-is.
- **Obsoletes ≠ Updates.** RFC 9113 also *updates* other documents and IANA registries (e.g., it moves the ALPN, HTTP/2 Frame Type, HTTP/2 Settings, HTTP/2 Error Code and HTTP Method registry references from RFC 7540 to itself; it marks the `HTTP2-Settings` header field registration and the `h2c` upgrade token as obsolete). Those are update/registry actions, not additions to the Obsoletes list.

## 4. Qualification on "current"

"Current" here means: the latest published IETF Standards Track RFC that specifies HTTP/2 itself, as of the sources consulted (fetched 2026-11-16). RFC 9113 is that document; no successor RFC obsoleting RFC 9113 appears in any consulted source. HTTP/2 has exactly one prior specification (RFC 7540) plus one amending document (RFC 8740), so the revision lineage is short and fully accounted for above.

**Re-verification procedure** (cheap, and the only thing that could change this answer): open <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/> and read the header block. If the page shows "Obsoleted by: RFC NNNN" or the `Obsoletes:` line differs from `7540, 8740`, the answer above is superseded and must be updated to RFC NNNN and that document's own `Obsoletes:` list. Equivalently, check <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/> or the RFC Editor's HTTP/2 subject page at <https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/>.

quotes.whole:
Kate Dearden
Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State
19th March 2026
Department for Business and Trade
Explanatory Note
(This note is not part of the Regulations)
These Regulations amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (“the 2015 Regulations”) (S.I. 2015/621). These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.
Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (regulation 4 of the 2015 Regulations).
Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
Regulation 2(3)(b) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are under the age of 18 from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(c) of the 2015 Regulations).
The apprenticeship rate applies to workers within regulation 5(1)(a) and (b) of the 2015 Regulations. Regulation 2(3)(c) of these Regulations increases the rate for such workers from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(d) of the 2015 Regulations).

Impact Assessments generally accompany all UK Government interventions of a regulatory nature that affect the private sector, civil society organisations and public services. They apply regardless of whether the regulation originates from a domestic or international source and can accompany primary (Acts etc) and secondary legislation (SIs). An Impact Assessment allows those with an interest in the policy area to understand:
Why the government is proposing to intervene;
The main options the government is considering, and which one is preferred;
How and to what extent new policies may impact on them; and,
The estimated costs and benefits of proposed measures.

Balancing all of these factors, we recommend an NLW increase of 4.1 per cent to £12.71 (a 50 pence per hour increase). This increase meets the Government’s target of two-thirds of median earnings for those aged 21 and over in 2026, reflects prevailing economic and business conditions, and exceeds expected inflation between April 2026 and April 2027, giving workers a real-terms pay rise.
2. Youth rates of the National Minimum Wage
The remit sets out the Government’s desire to balance its ambition to lower the NLW age of entitlement to 18 with its concern about current levels of youth unemployment.
The youth labour market is of concern to us. A “low hire, low fire” labour market is a challenge for young people as they are more dependent on vacancies. Older workers are more likely to already be in work and so are more protected in a “low fire” labour market. There has also been a concerning rise in the rate of young people not in education, employment or training (NEET).

We are alert to concerns about young people’s employment prospects
In making its recommendations for the 18-20 Year Old Rate, the Commission pays particular attention to whether increases in the youth rates have caused youth employment to fall.
While the Commission recognises that labour market outcomes for young people have deteriorated over the past two years, we are not aware of any robust evidence that higher youth rates have contributed to these falls. However, this remains an important question to ask.
Outcomes for young people are largely driven by the recent trends in the industries in which they work. Hospitality and retail are particularly important as they are the largest employers of young people. The tight labour market that followed the pandemic meant businesses (particularly in hospitality) struggled to find workers and so recruited more young people. Subsequently, labour market conditions have weakened and youth employment has fallen.

verdict.summary:
# UK statutory minimum wage rates effective 1 April 2026 — HR briefing note

## 1. Headline answers

| # | Ask | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 Mar 2026) | Cash increase | % increase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **National Living Wage (NLW), workers aged 21 and over** | **£12.71 per hour** | £12.21 | £0.50 | 4.1% |
| 2 | **National Minimum Wage (NMW), 18–20 Year Old Rate** | **£10.85 per hour** | £10.00 | £0.85 | 8.5% |

Both figures are **confirmed statutory rates**, not forecasts or projections. They apply in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland (SI 2026/357 extends to all four) and take effect **1 April 2026**. They remain in force until the next annual uprating on 1 April 2027.

## 2. Authority and verification trail

Use in this order of precedence:

1. **Primary legislation (operative law):** The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357, made 19 March 2026, coming into force 1 April 2026. Regulation 2(2) substitutes "£12.21" with "**£12.71**" in regulation 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (the NLW rate). Regulation 2(3)(a) substitutes "£10.00" with "**£10.85**" in regulation 4A(1)(b) (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21). Signed by Kate Dearden, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Business and Trade.
2. **Government announcement:** GOV.UK, "Minimum wage rates for 2026" (Low Pay Commission advice to Government), published 26 November 2025 — states the Government announced the 2026 increases and **accepted the LPC's recommendations in full**.
3. **Operational guidance:** GOV.UK, "National Minimum Wage rates" — live rates table, April 2026 row: 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; under 18 £8.00; apprentice £8.00.
4. **LPC impact report:** "The National Minimum Wage in 2026", published 1 April 2026 — restates the same table and confirms increases follow the LPC's October 2025 recommendations.

All four agree on both requested figures; there is no conflicting value in the record.

## 3. Full April 2026 rate card (for payroll configuration)

| Band | Rate from 1 Apr 2026 | Increase | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 / hour | £0.50 | 4.1% |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 / hour | £0.85 | 8.5% |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 / hour | £0.45 | 6.0% |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 / hour | £0.45 | 6.0% |
| Accommodation Offset | £11.10 **per day** | £0.44 | 4.1% |

Note the unit change on the accommodation offset: it is a **daily** cap on the amount an employer may deduct from pay for accommodation, not an hourly rate. Do not load it into an hourly-rate field in the payroll system.

## 4. Rules HR must apply alongside the headline figures

**Age band, not job role, drives the rate.**
- NLW applies to workers aged **21 and over** (the age of entitlement moved from 23 to 21 with effect from 1 April 2024 and remains at 21 through April 2026).
- The 18–20 Year Old Rate applies to workers aged **18 or over but not yet 21**.
- A worker moves to the higher band on their **21st birthday**, not at the following 1 April. Payroll must be driven by date of birth, not by a manual band flag set once a year.
- Workers under 18 (above school leaving age) are on the 16–17 Year Old Rate; apprentices have their own rules (below).

**Apprentices.** The apprentice rate (£8.00) applies only if the apprentice is **aged under 19**, or is **aged 19 or over and in the first year** of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 19+ who has completed the first year moves to the full rate for their age — e.g. an apprentice aged 21 who has finished year one is entitled to £12.71.

**What counts toward the minimum.** Pay for NMW/NLW purposes includes most pay elements but excludes tips, service charge, overtime premium, unsocial-hours premium, and expenses. Deductions for uniforms, tools, equipment, training or breakages, and any required payment to the employer, reduce *disposable* pay and can push an apparently compliant rate below the statutory floor. **Salary sacrifice must not take pay below the applicable minimum** — check pension and cycle-to-work arrangements against £12.71/£10.85, not against the pre-April figures.

**Salaried and annualised-hours staff.** For monthly-salaried employees, verify compliance by dividing actual pay by actual hours worked in each pay period. Term-time-only and annualised-hours contracts are the highest-risk groups at an 8.5% youth-rate increase.

**Accommodation.** Where accommodation is provided, the employer may deduct no more than £11.10 per day; anything above that counts as a deduction from pay and risks breaching the minimum.

**Records.** Keep NMW/NLW records for **at least six years** — sufficient to show pay, hours, deductions and the age band applied for every worker.

## 5. HR action checklist for the 1 April 2026 uplift

1. **Payroll configuration** — load all five figures above, effective 1 April 2026; run a parallel test payroll before the live run; confirm the pro-rata treatment for anyone whose pay period straddles 31 March / 1 April.
2. **Full-population sweep** — extract every worker paid at or near the floor and re-test against the new rate, including commission-only, piece-rate, zero-hours and agency-supplied staff. The 8.5% uplift on the 18–20 band is the larger shock; 18–20s who were comfortably above £10.00 may now be below £10.85.
3. **Age-band audit** — reconcile date of birth to rate code for every worker aged 17–22; correct any worker who turned 21 but was left on the youth rate.
4. **Differential compression** — where team members or supervisors were paid a premium above the old floor, check whether the uplift has flattened differentials; decide and document whether to preserve them (retention risk sits with newly hired supervisors earning close to their reports).
5. **Contracts and offer letters** — update template rates, salary bands and any clause referencing the NLW/NMW by figure rather than by reference to statute.
6. **Communications** — brief line managers before the change lands in payslips; issue a short employee note explaining the increase and the effective date.
7. **Budgeting** — model the cost at 4.1% on the 21+ population and 8.5% on the 18–20 population, plus the knock-on effect on employer National Insurance, pension contributions and any pay scales contractually linked to the minimum wage.
8. **Risk** — underpayment exposes the employer to arrears plus a penalty of up to 200% of arrears (capped per worker), public naming, and director disqualification consideration. Treat any identified underpayment as remediable immediately, with arrears backdated to 1 April 2026.

## 6. Forward-planning note (do not confuse with the answer)

The same GOV.UK rates table already shows the **April 2027** row: £13.21 (21+), £11.27 (18–20), £8.31 (16–17 and apprentice). Treat these as published forward figures for multi-year budgeting only; the rates that answer this request, and the only rates legally in force from 1 April 2026, are **£12.71** and **£10.85**.

## 7. What these figures are not

- They are **not** the voluntary "Real Living Wage" published by the Living Wage Foundation, which is set independently of Government, is higher, and is not a statutory minimum. No figure for it is stated here; verify separately if it is needed for accreditation or supplier policy.
- They are **not** London-weighted — there is no statutory regional or London rate.
- They are **not** net pay, and take no account of tax, National Insurance or employer-specific enhancements.
- They are **not** the rate for 16–17 year olds, apprentices, or the accommodation offset, each of which is listed separately above.

quotes.whole:
What has changed?
Short-haul Exception
Expands the short-haul exception to 150 air-miles and allows a 14-hour work shift to take place as part of the exception.
Adverse Driving Conditions Exception
Expands the driving window during adverse driving conditions by up to an additional 2 hours.
30-Minute Break Requirement
Requires break of at least 30 consecutive minutes after 8 cumulative hours of driving time (instead of on-duty time) and allows an on-duty/not driving period to qualify as the required break.
Sleeper Berth Provision
Modifies the sleeper berth exception to allow a driver to meet the 10-hour minimum off-duty requirement by spending at least 7 hours of that period in the berth combined with a minimum off-duty period of at least 2 hours spent inside or outside the berth, provided the two periods total at least 10 hours. When used together as specified, neither qualify period counts against the 14-hour driving window.
Educational Tool for Hours of Service (ETHOS)
FMCSA launched a new online tool that allows users to enter driver records of duty status to see if there are potential violations with the new hours of service regulations.

verdict.summary:
Governing provision: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), the FMCSA short-haul exception to the record-of-duty-status requirement (current eCFR text; the 2020 HOS final rule expanded the exception from 100 air miles/12 hours to 150 air miles/14 hours).

Answer 1 — Radius: The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation states this as "150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles)." The regulatory unit is air miles; 150 air miles is approximately 172.6 statute miles, not 150 statute miles.

Answer 2 — Release from work: The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The 14-hour period runs consecutively from the time the driver comes on duty following the required off-duty period; it is not cumulative on-duty time summed across shifts.

Supporting conditions in 395.1(e)(1):
- The driver must operate within the 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location.
- Except for a driver-salesperson, the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.
- A property-carrying CMV driver must have at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty.
- A passenger-carrying CMV driver must have at least 8 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty.
- The motor carrier must maintain and retain for 6 months accurate time records showing the time the driver reports for duty each day, total hours on duty each day, time released from duty each day, and, for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, total time for the preceding 7 days under 395.8(j)(2).

Both the property-carrying and passenger-carrying versions of 395.1(e)(1) use the same 150-air-mile radius and the same 14-consecutive-hour return-and-release deadline. The difference between the two versions is the off-duty minimum: 10 consecutive hours for property-carrying drivers and 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying drivers.

The exception relieves the driver of the RODS and ELD requirements of 395.8 and 395.11; it does not relieve the driver of all hours-of-service obligations. If the driver exceeds the 150-air-mile radius or is not returned and released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception is unavailable for that day and a record of duty status is required.

Note on the separate non-CDL property-carrying exception: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(2) also uses a 150 air-mile radius, but its hour structure is not a single 14-hour release rule. It prohibits driving after the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days and after the 16th hour after coming on duty on 2 days of any period of 7 consecutive days, with return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour. The two answers above address the 395.1(e)(1) short-haul exception described in the question.
